sense: a part of a play, film or story

terms.gloss: a passage, a part of a work
terms.grammar: noun, second declension; plural locī for passages of a book
evidence: Cic. Fin. 1.7: locōs quōsdam trānsferam (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Classical Latin has no word for a scene as a division of a play; locus is the word for a passage or part of any work, and serves for a scene in a play or a film. Its first sense is a place (see position); the plural for passages is locī, for places mostly loca (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: a scene, as a division of a play
evidence: Lewis & Short, s.v. scaena (the stage only)
terms.comment: Classically the stage, and so the theatre and the public eye (scaenae servīre, to live in the public eye, Cic. ad Brut. 8.2); printed editions divide plays into āctūs and scaenae, but no ancient author uses the word of a part of a play.

phrases.latin: Quī locus fābulae tibi maximē placuit?
phrases.english: Which scene in the play did you like best?

scaena-scene.html: Lewis & Short gives scaena only as the stage, the theatre, the public stage and outward show; the sense “a scene” comes from the act-and-scene divisions of printed editions. We have not found it in Traupman or Morgan–Owens.
